name: Lancaster
tagline: Britain's principal night bomber of WWII and the aircraft of the Dambusters raid. Its cavernous 33-foot bomb bay could carry heavier loads than any other European bomber, from 4,000 lb 'Cookies' to the 22,000 lb Grand Slam, the heaviest weapon dropped in the war.
history:
The Lancaster was born from failure: Avro's twin-engined Manchester of 1939 was crippled by its unreliable Rolls-Royce Vulture engines, and chief designer Roy Chadwick's response - stretching the wing and fitting four proven Merlins instead - transformed a deathtrap into the war's finest heavy bomber. The prototype flew on 9 January 1941 and No. 44 Squadron flew the first operational sorties in March 1942.

The aircraft's defining night came on 16-17 May 1943, when nineteen specially modified Lancasters of the newly formed No. 617 Squadron, led by 24-year-old Wing Commander Guy Gibson, attacked the Ruhr dams with Barnes Wallis's 'bouncing bombs', breaching the Möhne and Eder dams at a cost of eight aircraft and 53 men - the raid that made both the squadron and the aircraft immortal. Lancasters went on to sink the battleship Tirpitz with 12,000 lb Tallboy bombs in November 1944, and in the war's final weeks flew Operation Manna food drops to starving Dutch civilians and repatriated 74,000 prisoners of war.

Postwar, Lancasters served in maritime patrol into the 1950s (France retired the last military examples in 1964), and the type evolved into the Lincoln bomber, the Lancastrian airliner and the Shackleton patrol aircraft, whose airframes flew with the RAF until 1991 - a Chadwick lineage of exactly fifty years. PA474, built in 1945 and today one of the BBMF's crown jewels, entered a scheduled major maintenance programme in late 2025 to keep her flying for decades more.

quickFacts: The Lancaster grew out of a failure - it was essentially Avro's disastrous twin-engined Manchester redesigned around four Merlins, and became the best heavy bomber of the war.
Its 33-foot bomb bay could carry the 22,000 lb Grand Slam, the heaviest bomb dropped by any aircraft in WWII - no other European bomber came close.
Of 7,377 Lancasters built, 3,249 were lost in action; more than 55,000 Bomber Command aircrew were killed, at an average age of just 22.
The Dambusters of No. 617 Squadron breached the Möhne and Eder dams in May 1943 flying Lancasters at 60 feet, at night, at exactly 232 mph - the height set by two spotlights converging on the water.
Lancasters sank the German battleship Tirpitz in November 1944 with 12,000 lb Tallboy earthquake bombs.
Only two of the 7,377 still fly: Britain's PA474 and Canada's FM213 - their 2014 joint tour was the first time two Lancasters had flown together in over 50 years.
In the war's final days Lancasters swapped bombs for food, dropping over 6,600 tons of supplies to starving Dutch civilians in Operation Manna.

overview: The Avro Lancaster is a four-engine heavy bomber built for RAF Bomber Command during the Second World War. Developed from the failed twin-engine Manchester, it first flew in January 1941 and went on to carry roughly two-thirds of Bomber Command's total bomb tonnage against Germany.{{ref:wiki-lanc}}

Its 33-foot unobstructed bomb bay let it carry weapons no other Allied bomber could, from the bouncing bombs of the 1943 Dambusters raid to the 22,000 lb Grand Slam, the heaviest bomb of the war. Some 7,377 were built, and 44% of Lancaster aircrew did not survive their service.{{ref:wiki-lanc}}

sections.heading: Origins & Concept
paragraphs: The Manchester of 1940 had a superb airframe strapped to two catastrophes: Rolls-Royce Vulture engines that failed with lethal regularity. Chadwick's team salvaged the design in months - a longer wing, four proven Merlins - and the prototype Lancaster flew in January 1941 to immediate acclaim from everyone who touched it.{{ref:wiki-lanc}}

The transformation was total: where the Manchester struggled, the Lancaster hauled 14,000 lb of bombs to Berlin, climbed on three engines, and possessed the huge unobstructed 33-foot bomb bay that would define its career - the feature that let it carry weapons no other Allied aircraft could contemplate.{{ref:wiki-lanc}}

sections.heading: Combat History
paragraphs: From 1942 the Lancaster was the spearhead of the RAF's night offensive: the thousand-bomber raids, the Battle of the Ruhr, the firestorm at Hamburg, the long bloody winter over Berlin. Lancasters flew some 156,000 sorties and dropped over 600,000 tons of bombs - roughly two-thirds of Bomber Command's entire war tonnage - at a cost of more than 3,200 aircraft lost.{{ref:wiki-lanc}}

Its fame crystallised on one May night in 1943, when 617 Squadron's specially modified Lancasters skimmed German reservoirs at 60 feet to deliver Barnes Wallis's bouncing bombs into the Möhne and Eder dams - Operation Chastise, the Dambusters, the most storied precision raid of the war.{{ref:wiki-chastise}}

The bomb bay kept rewriting the target list: 12,000 lb Tallboys that sank the Tirpitz in November 1944, and the 22,000 lb Grand Slam - the heaviest bomb of the war, carried by no other aircraft - that brought down viaducts and U-boat pens in 1945. The Lancaster's war ended gently: Operation Manna food drops to starving Holland, and flights home packed with liberated prisoners.{{ref:wiki-lanc}}

sections.heading: Design & Engineering
paragraphs: The Lancaster was a bomb bay with an aircraft attached: 33 feet of unobstructed volume that swallowed loads - a 4,000 lb 'cookie' plus incendiaries, an 8,000 lb blockbuster, eventually the ten-ton Grand Slam (with doors removed) - that the B-17 with its bomb load an ocean away could not approach. Typical Lancaster loads ran two to three times a Flying Fortress's over Germany.{{ref:wiki-lanc}}

Everything else served that bay. Four Merlins gave honest performance and battle redundancy; eight .303 guns in three turrets gave thin protection; and the fuselage's spartan interior - one main spar to clamber over, temperatures far below freezing, minimal survival equipment - reflected an aircraft designed to deliver bombs, not to protect its crew. Even so, damaged Lancasters were renowned for bringing crews home.{{ref:iwm-lanc}}

sections.heading: Development
paragraphs: 7,377 Lancasters were built - most from Avro's Manchester-area plants, 430 by Victory Aircraft in Canada, whose 'Lancaster X' line seeded the postwar Canadian aviation industry. Variants stayed minimal: the design was right, and wartime Britain built what worked.{{ref:wiki-lanc}}

Its lineage carried on: the Lincoln bomber, the York transport, and the Shackleton maritime patroller that flew for the RAF until 1991 - Lancaster DNA on patrol half a century after the prototype. The airliner Lancastrian even pioneered postwar transatlantic routes.{{ref:wiki-lanc}}

sections.heading: Legacy
paragraphs: The Lancaster carries the whole weight of the strategic bombing debate - the decisive contribution and the cities burned, valour and horror in one airframe. Britain took decades to memorialise Bomber Command's dead; the Lancaster, through it all, remained the crews' untarnished symbol of what they endured together.{{ref:iwm-lanc}}

Two still fly - the Battle of Britain Memorial Flight's PA474 and Canada's 'Vera' - and their appearance over any airfield stops it cold. Seventeen survive complete; each is, in effect, a national memorial with wings.{{ref:bbmf-lanc}}

accidentsAndIncidents.title: Dambusters Raid losses (Operation Chastise)
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: During 617 Squadron's dam-busting raid on the Ruhr, eight of the nineteen Lancasters that took part were shot down or lost, killing 53 of 133 aircrew.

accidentsAndIncidents.title: Shot down near Düsseldorf
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: Lancaster ND342, returning from a raid on the Krupp steelworks at Essen, was shot down by a German night fighter and crashed near Düsseldorf. Ten of the thirteen crew were killed; the rest became prisoners of war.

accidentsAndIncidents.title: Crash into Montecristo island
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: Lancaster TX269, flying from Malta to Cornwall during a joint exercise, struck the island of Montecristo at low altitude and burned. All seven aboard were killed.

accidentsAndIncidents.title: Engine failure crash at Luqa
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: A search-and-rescue Lancaster lost an engine shortly after takeoff from RAF Luqa, Malta, and crashed into a residential street. Three of the four crew and one person on the ground were killed.

accidentsAndIncidents.title: BBMF Lancaster in-flight engine fire
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: PA474, one of only two airworthy Lancasters, suffered an engine fire shortly after taking off from RAF Coningsby. The crew shut the engine down and landed safely; the engine and wing were rebuilt and the aircraft returned to display flying.
